Affective polarization in these early elections is distinctively low, thus pulling down the fit line at the beginning of the time trend. If we were to look only at the period analyzed by Boxell et al.-the eleven data points from 1980 to 2017-we would find no significant polarization trend for Germany. Overall, this finding highlights the added value of the longer time series offered by our data. Please refer to the "On the divergence of Germany's estimates between our data and Boxell, Gentzkow, and Shapiro (2021)" Supplementary Material section for a more detailed comparison.

Title: Political Polarization and Wellbeing: Investigating Potential Intrapersonal Harm From Affective Polarization
Snippet: While the findings from prior research support a theoretical argument for how affective polarization could exert a negative impact on social, mental, and physical wellbeing, such effects have not been investigated using analyses that are suitable for investigating causality. Thus, the claim that affective polarization exerts an inward harm and that 'resentment is like drinking poison' (Nelson, 2022, p. 508) has not yet been supported. We perform the first investigation of the intrapersonal harms of affective polarization using designs and analyses suitable for investigating causal effects. 

The present six-wave longitudinal study, which ran for three months preceding the 2024 US presidential election, investigated the effect of affective polarization on social support, stress, and health, using singleindicator random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs; Mulder & Hamaker, 2021). The RI-CLPM is well-suited for investigating causality because it establishes temporal precedence in estimating effects, which cannot be inferred from standard cross-sectional designs. 

As in standard cross-lagged panel models, the RI-CLPM models the autoregressive effects over time, and thus controls for the carry-over effects of variables with themselves. The inclusion of the random intercepts allows the RI-CLPM to partial-out stable betweenperson differences and model the within-person relationships between variables more accurately, whereas the traditional cross-lagged panel model confuses interindividual associations for intraindividual processes (Hamaker, Kuiper & Grasman, 2015). The results of between-person analyses often do not reflect the actual relationships between variables within individuals when there are both stable traits and state level components to the variance (Hamaker, 2023). Because of this, we can assume that the crosslagged coefficients from an RI-CLPM more accurately reflect causal relationships (Lucas, 2023), though we still cannot make strong causal claims-rather, we rely on a weaker claim akin to Granger causality (Bressler & Seth, 2011;Hamaker, Kuiper & Grasman, 2015). The RI-CLPM is one method of analysis which can better address questions of causality from non-experimental data.

snippet.text:
While the findings from prior research support a theoretical argument for how affective polarization could exert a negative impact on social, mental, and physical wellbeing, such effects have not been investigated using analyses that are suitable for investigating causality. Thus, the claim that affective polarization exerts an inward harm and that 'resentment is like drinking poison' (Nelson, 2022, p. 508) has not yet been supported. We perform the first investigation of the intrapersonal harms of affective polarization using designs and analyses suitable for investigating causal effects. 

The present six-wave longitudinal study, which ran for three months preceding the 2024 US presidential election, investigated the effect of affective polarization on social support, stress, and health, using singleindicator random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs; Mulder & Hamaker, 2021). The RI-CLPM is well-suited for investigating causality because it establishes temporal precedence in estimating effects, which cannot be inferred from standard cross-sectional designs. 

As in standard cross-lagged panel models, the RI-CLPM models the autoregressive effects over time, and thus controls for the carry-over effects of variables with themselves. The inclusion of the random intercepts allows the RI-CLPM to partial-out stable betweenperson differences and model the within-person relationships between variables more accurately, whereas the traditional cross-lagged panel model confuses interindividual associations for intraindividual processes (Hamaker, Kuiper & Grasman, 2015). The results of between-person analyses often do not reflect the actual relationships between variables within individuals when there are both stable traits and state level components to the variance (Hamaker, 2023). Because of this, we can assume that the crosslagged coefficients from an RI-CLPM more accurately reflect causal relationships (Lucas, 2023), though we still cannot make strong causal claims-rather, we rely on a weaker claim akin to Granger causality (Bressler & Seth, 2011;Hamaker, Kuiper & Grasman, 2015). The RI-CLPM is one method of analysis which can better address questions of causality from non-experimental data.

Title: Who Dislikes Whom? Affective Polarization between Pairs of Parties in Western Democracies
Snippet: The Role of Elite Ideological and Issue-Based Disagreements Scholars of US polarization have extensively analyzed the relationship between elite-level ideological polarization and mass-level affective polarization. Rogowski and Sutherland (2015) show that greater ideological differences between US candidates intensify affective polarization (see also Lelkes 2021), while Abramowitz and Webster (2017) find that partisans' affective evaluations respond to perceived ideological distance. Comparatively, Westwood et al. (2018) demonstrate that partisans discriminate more against out-partisans that are farther away from them ideologically. There is a growing agreement that affective polarization is rooted, at least partially, in policy disagreements (Orr and Huber 2020). 

Yet, an agreement does not yet imply full consensus, as alternative accounts de-emphasize ideological disputes. From the perspective of social identity theory, affective polarization reflects partisans' psychological needs to enhance their group's status (Huddy, Bankert, and Davies 2018). Shifting the emphasis from ideological disagreements to group identities, this suggests that US affective polarization is primarily driven by the overlap of religious, racial, and partisan identities, rather than ideology (Mason 2018). Levendusky and Stecula (2021, 1, emphasis in the original) summarize this view by noting that "even when the parties agree on the issues, they still dislike and distrust one another-this is not simply a difference of opinion, but is rather something deeper." We evaluate this relationship across pairs of parties: 

The Left-Right ideology hypothesis (H1): Greater elite ideological distance between pairs of parties predicts greater affective polarization between these parties' supporters. 

Issue-based elite polarization: economics and culture While comparative affective polarization research emphasizes elite disagreements on Left-Right ideology (see, for example, Reiljan 2020; Wagner 2021), there is a rationale for distinguishing between two cross-cutting dimensions that largely structure Western politics: economics and culture (Hooghe and Marks 2017;Kitschelt 1994;Kriesi et al. 2006;Kriesi et al. 2008).

Title: Beyond Observational Relationships: Evidence from a Ten-Country Experiment that Policy Disputes Cause Affective Polarization
Snippet: Concerns over growing hostility across party linesthat is, affective polarization (Iyengar et al. 2012(Iyengar et al. , 2019) ) have proliferated in recent years. These concerns originated in the American context, where scholars have argued that affective polarization is linked to negative outcomes such as low trust in government and the erosion of democratic commitments (Druckman et al. 2021(Druckman et al. , 2023;;Graham and Svolik 2020;Hetherington and Rudolph 2015;Kingzette et al. 2021;Levendusky and Stecula 2021), although evidence of its effects on democratic norms is mixed (Broockman et al. 2023;Voelkel et al. 2023). Comparative scholarship reports intense affective polarization across many Western polities (Boxell et al. 2024;Gidron et al. 2020;Reiljan 2020;Wagner 2021Wagner , 2024)). 

Research on American politics analyzes the relationship between affective polarization and ideological disputes (Lelkes 2021;Orr and Huber 2020), and there is comparative evidence that cultural disagreements are increasingly associated with negative out-party affect (Gidron et al. 2023;Harteveld 2021). Yet we lack comparative causal evidence on these relationships. Moreover, prior work has not yet parsed out which specific issues drive this process. 

We experimentally evaluate whether cultural and economic disputes intensify partisan animosity by analyzing novel survey data collected across ten Western publics. The survey includes a priming experiment asking some respondents to provide open-ended answers to a question about economic policy disagreements, and others to discuss cultural disagreements, while respondents in the control group receive a non-political prompt. We find that respondents in the economic and cultural priming conditions express significantly greater distrust of partisan opponents, compared to those in the control group, and that respondents who discuss immigration in their open-ended answers express greater distrust towards out-partisans, particularly those who are primed to view immigration through a cultural lens. The latter effect is entirely driven by those right-wing respondents who discussed immigration.

Title: Micropolarization: performances of antagonism and struggles for recognition during the COVID-19 pandemic
Snippet: We mean antagonistic conflict in a broad sense, akin to how Gøtzsche-Astrup (2022) theorizes the experience of contention as expression of the potential of conflict. This experience involves engaging with the public drama, envisioning oneself as part of collective struggles, occasionally participating through online discussions, activism, voting, etc. It also involves directly confronting opponents, whether strangers, acquaintances, or friends and family. 

Political conflict is crucial in understanding affective polarization, as feelings of hostility not only cause conflict but also stem from prior conflicts. Antagonistic conflict is defined in creating seemingly insurmountable differences between opponents, leading to friend/enemy distinctions, moral attributions, and associated feelings. Existing research often measures affective polarization through survey "thermometer ratings" and social distance measures (tolerance of inter-party marriage of one's child [see Druckman and Levendusky 2019]), providing insights into the extent of divisions over time and across societies. However, we learn little about the affective experience of polarization, feeling rejected by others and its implications for relationships. Furthermore, the emotions and divisions triggered by political elites, their communication, and influence on perceptions and interpersonal political discord need attention. Elite polarization (McCarty et al. 2006) not only hampers decisionmaking (Binder 2015) but also fosters perceptions of divisions through effective partisan sorting (Levendusky 2010). Likewise, media representations of polarization also strengthen these perceptions (Levendusky 2013;Levendusky and Malhotra 2016;Robison and Mullinix 2016). Based on the degree to which these representations are factually unwarranted, some scholars qualify such mediated perceptions as "false polarization" (Fernbach and Van Boven 2022). To us, such perceptions are relevant as they shape audience experiences and materialize in "deep stories" (Hochschild 2016), regardless of their factual justification. 

Polarization in and through communication is a yet under-researched area, though a number of studies focused on the polarizing effects of exposure to diverse and divided encounters on social media (e.g., Bail et al. 2018;Banks et al. 2021).

Title: Elite Cooperation and Affective Polarization: Evidence From German Coalitions
Snippet: Affective polarization has emerged as an important lens through which to understand the nature of political competition (Iyengar et al., 2019). Though precise definitions differ, the term generally refers to the extent to which party supporters feel close to and warmly towards their own party and feel distant from and cold towards (the supporters of) rival parties (Iyengar et al., 2012). One reason affective polarization has been the focus of much recent research is that it is seen as a potential danger for democratic quality and stability (e.g. Kingzette et al., 2021;McCoy and Somer, 2019;cf. Broockman et al., 2022). As a result, various ways of decreasing affective polarization have been proposed and examined (see Hartman et al., 2022;Voelkel et al., 2022). 

In this article, we focus on how elite signals can influence levels of affective polarization (Bassan-Nygate and Weiss, 2022;Huddy and Yair, 2021). Elite signals might provide an important account of why affective polarization differs over time and across countries. In time periods or countries where elites signal interparty conflict and the inability to compromise, party supporters may develop higher levels of affective polarization. For example, elite ideological polarization is correlated with voter-level affective polarization (Rogowski and Sutherland, 2016), and affective polarization increases around elections (Bassan-Nygate and Weiss, 2022;Hernandez et al., 2021;Singh and Thornton, 2019). This also means that elite signals could provide a key way of reducing affective polarization. If elites are willing to show that they can and want to work with rivals, this could reduce enmity between rival political camps (Huddy and Yair, 2021). Of course, in highly affectively polarized systems, any cooperation might already be beyond the pale in the first place (think of the scarcity of partisan compromise in the United States). Still, many political systems (especially those with proportional representation) are still characterized by the institutional need, as well as some political willingness, to work together. We argue that whether and how they do so affects citizens' evaluations of political opponents.

Title: Learning to Like the Enemy: Moral Learning Reduces Affective Polarization
Snippet: As affective polarization, an identity-defining attitude (Dias & Lelkes, 2022), has increased, treatments mitigating the disapproval of political opponents are sorely needed. Our results across three experiments showed that exposure to moral behaviors of out-party members effectively reduces polarization. These findings are important for policymakers and civil society interested in fighting affective polarization. Highlighting the moral behavior of out-party members and thereby emphasizing the joint value base of all citizens could be effectively implemented in future campaigns or educational programs aiming to fight affective polarization. For example, social media clips can present real-life examples of people who put themselves in danger to help others while noting their political affiliation. Finally, the moral learning treatment can be applied to other conflict areas, such as post-war reconciliation or the reduction of prejudice.

snippet.text:
Concerns over growing hostility across party linesthat is, affective polarization (Iyengar et al. 2012(Iyengar et al. , 2019) ) have proliferated in recent years. These concerns originated in the American context, where scholars have argued that affective polarization is linked to negative outcomes such as low trust in government and the erosion of democratic commitments (Druckman et al. 2021(Druckman et al. , 2023;;Graham and Svolik 2020;Hetherington and Rudolph 2015;Kingzette et al. 2021;Levendusky and Stecula 2021), although evidence of its effects on democratic norms is mixed (Broockman et al. 2023;Voelkel et al. 2023). Comparative scholarship reports intense affective polarization across many Western polities (Boxell et al. 2024;Gidron et al. 2020;Reiljan 2020;Wagner 2021Wagner , 2024)). 

Research on American politics analyzes the relationship between affective polarization and ideological disputes (Lelkes 2021;Orr and Huber 2020), and there is comparative evidence that cultural disagreements are increasingly associated with negative out-party affect (Gidron et al. 2023;Harteveld 2021). Yet we lack comparative causal evidence on these relationships. Moreover, prior work has not yet parsed out which specific issues drive this process. 

We experimentally evaluate whether cultural and economic disputes intensify partisan animosity by analyzing novel survey data collected across ten Western publics. The survey includes a priming experiment asking some respondents to provide open-ended answers to a question about economic policy disagreements, and others to discuss cultural disagreements, while respondents in the control group receive a non-political prompt. We find that respondents in the economic and cultural priming conditions express significantly greater distrust of partisan opponents, compared to those in the control group, and that respondents who discuss immigration in their open-ended answers express greater distrust towards out-partisans, particularly those who are primed to view immigration through a cultural lens. The latter effect is entirely driven by those right-wing respondents who discussed immigration.

snippet.text:
We mean antagonistic conflict in a broad sense, akin to how Gøtzsche-Astrup (2022) theorizes the experience of contention as expression of the potential of conflict. This experience involves engaging with the public drama, envisioning oneself as part of collective struggles, occasionally participating through online discussions, activism, voting, etc. It also involves directly confronting opponents, whether strangers, acquaintances, or friends and family. 

Political conflict is crucial in understanding affective polarization, as feelings of hostility not only cause conflict but also stem from prior conflicts. Antagonistic conflict is defined in creating seemingly insurmountable differences between opponents, leading to friend/enemy distinctions, moral attributions, and associated feelings. Existing research often measures affective polarization through survey "thermometer ratings" and social distance measures (tolerance of inter-party marriage of one's child [see Druckman and Levendusky 2019]), providing insights into the extent of divisions over time and across societies. However, we learn little about the affective experience of polarization, feeling rejected by others and its implications for relationships. Furthermore, the emotions and divisions triggered by political elites, their communication, and influence on perceptions and interpersonal political discord need attention. Elite polarization (McCarty et al. 2006) not only hampers decisionmaking (Binder 2015) but also fosters perceptions of divisions through effective partisan sorting (Levendusky 2010). Likewise, media representations of polarization also strengthen these perceptions (Levendusky 2013;Levendusky and Malhotra 2016;Robison and Mullinix 2016). Based on the degree to which these representations are factually unwarranted, some scholars qualify such mediated perceptions as "false polarization" (Fernbach and Van Boven 2022). To us, such perceptions are relevant as they shape audience experiences and materialize in "deep stories" (Hochschild 2016), regardless of their factual justification. 

Polarization in and through communication is a yet under-researched area, though a number of studies focused on the polarizing effects of exposure to diverse and divided encounters on social media (e.g., Bail et al. 2018;Banks et al. 2021).

snippet.text:
Affective polarization has emerged as an important lens through which to understand the nature of political competition (Iyengar et al., 2019). Though precise definitions differ, the term generally refers to the extent to which party supporters feel close to and warmly towards their own party and feel distant from and cold towards (the supporters of) rival parties (Iyengar et al., 2012). One reason affective polarization has been the focus of much recent research is that it is seen as a potential danger for democratic quality and stability (e.g. Kingzette et al., 2021;McCoy and Somer, 2019;cf. Broockman et al., 2022). As a result, various ways of decreasing affective polarization have been proposed and examined (see Hartman et al., 2022;Voelkel et al., 2022). 

In this article, we focus on how elite signals can influence levels of affective polarization (Bassan-Nygate and Weiss, 2022;Huddy and Yair, 2021). Elite signals might provide an important account of why affective polarization differs over time and across countries. In time periods or countries where elites signal interparty conflict and the inability to compromise, party supporters may develop higher levels of affective polarization. For example, elite ideological polarization is correlated with voter-level affective polarization (Rogowski and Sutherland, 2016), and affective polarization increases around elections (Bassan-Nygate and Weiss, 2022;Hernandez et al., 2021;Singh and Thornton, 2019). This also means that elite signals could provide a key way of reducing affective polarization. If elites are willing to show that they can and want to work with rivals, this could reduce enmity between rival political camps (Huddy and Yair, 2021). Of course, in highly affectively polarized systems, any cooperation might already be beyond the pale in the first place (think of the scarcity of partisan compromise in the United States). Still, many political systems (especially those with proportional representation) are still characterized by the institutional need, as well as some political willingness, to work together. We argue that whether and how they do so affects citizens' evaluations of political opponents.

snippet.text: As affective polarization, an identity-defining attitude (Dias & Lelkes, 2022), has increased, treatments mitigating the disapproval of political opponents are sorely needed. Our results across three experiments showed that exposure to moral behaviors of out-party members effectively reduces polarization. These findings are important for policymakers and civil society interested in fighting affective polarization. Highlighting the moral behavior of out-party members and thereby emphasizing the joint value base of all citizens could be effectively implemented in future campaigns or educational programs aiming to fight affective polarization. For example, social media clips can present real-life examples of people who put themselves in danger to help others while noting their political affiliation. Finally, the moral learning treatment can be applied to other conflict areas, such as post-war reconciliation or the reduction of prejudice.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of what current research shows about whether elite affective polarization—operationalized as private feelings, public rhetoric, or strategic framing—differentially predicts mass polarization, and which mechanism tends to matter most.

# Concepts and Operationalizations

Affective polarization in the mass public is commonly proxied by privately expressed feelings such as warmth or disgust toward ingroups and outgroups (e.g., feeling thermometers), and by desires to socially distance from partisans of other parties; these instruments capture core affect but often abstract from the communicative context in which feelings are performed and interpreted <cite id="3478dea0-0">Affective polarization is typically measured with instruments such as the “feeling thermometer,” and the difference between warmth toward ingroups and outgroups is treated as a proxy; however, these survey measures abstract from the identity performances through which people publicly signal views, and judgments depend heavily on framing and question order</cite>. In comparative and longitudinal analyses across Western democracies, affective polarization has become more heavily characterized by “out-party hate” relative to “in-party love,” indicating a pronounced affective backdrop against which elite signals operate <cite id="3478dea0-2">A generalized decline of out-party evaluations and a growing prevalence of out-party hate versus in-party love over time shows contemporary affective polarization is more heavily characterized by disproportionate out-group dislike</cite>.

# Private Feelings and Affect as Predictors

Experimental and physiological work shows that exposure to political rhetoric elicits affect that predicts opinion change, with attitude extremity and incongruence amplifying arousal and negative affect; importantly, affective responses can lead to change even when self-reported emotions are held constant, underscoring their causal potency as predictors of downstream polarization dynamics <cite id="16e5448b-0">People with extreme attitudes experience more arousal in response to political rhetoric, and rhetoric incongruent with prior attitudes evokes negative affect; affective responses lead to opinion change independent of self-reported emotions</cite>. This establishes a mechanism by which private feelings among elites (e.g., moral outrage, contempt) communicated in speech and imagery can seed and amplify negative affect in mass audiences, which in turn predicts greater social distance and antagonism toward out-partisans <cite id="3478dea0-0">Surveys estimate mental states but overlook identity performances through which judgments are made, which are foundational for perceiving alignment and opposition and constructing shared opinion structures that make polarization possible</cite>. The background rise in out-party hate suggests that when elite cues emphasize moral violations and antagonistic identities, mass negative affect is more likely to be sustained or intensified <cite id="3478dea0-2">Out-party hate has grown relative to in-party love over time, indicating a disproportionate weight of out-group dislike</cite>.

# Public Rhetoric: Tone, Moral Signals, and Depolarization

Randomized experiments show that elite rhetoric need not polarize. Politicians’ congenial, respectful messages about opponents reduce citizens’ negative emotions toward out-partisans and their desire to socially distance from them, without requiring partisan alignment or high trust; this indicates a causal depolarizing effect of positive elite rhetoric targeting affect and intergroup attitudes <cite id="3478dea0-1">Politicians’ congenial messages significantly reduce citizens’ negative emotions toward outpartisans and desire to socially distance, independent of politician–citizen alignment and without necessarily requiring high political trust</cite>. Title: How language divides: Asymmetries in the differentiating power of opinion discourse
Snippet: Despite its diversity, research on polarization in social psychology shares a common methodological feature: heavy reliance on survey responses. Affective polarization (Iyengar et al., 2012) is typically measured using instruments such as the "feeling thermometer" (Gidron et al., 2022), while political and opinion polarization are assessed through rating scales capturing attitudes toward social groups or policy positions. Although polarization is "most properly understood as a description of the distribution of a population" (Bakker & Lelkes, 2024, p. 419), it is frequently operationalized as an individual-difference variable. Participants are asked to rate how warm or cold they feel toward ingroups and outgroups, and the difference between these ratings is treated as a proxy for polarization (e.g., Kingzette et al., 2021;Wakefield & Wakefield, 2023). These scores are then used as predictors or outcomes in linear models, abstracting polarization from its social and communicative context. 

This approach allows researchers to observe patterns of attitudinal congruence and divergence, but it overlooks how people judge group affiliation and opinion similarity in everyday settings (cf. Durrheim, 2022;Durrheim et al., 2016). By eliciting privately expressed attitudes, surveys estimate mental states within a broader distribution, yet they do not examine the identity performances (Klein et al., 2007) through which individuals publicly signal their views and interpret those of others. What is measured depends heavily on how categories are constructed and interpreted-processes that remain opaque within the instrument itself. In everyday interaction, individuals contradict themselves, articulate nuanced positions, and adjust their views across contexts.

Strategic framing by elites channels content into affect-laden moral schemas (e.g., care/harm, fairness/comparison, loyalty/in-group, authority/respect, sanctity/purity), with systematic reviews emphasizing that outcomes should distinguish cognitive, perceived, and affective polarization and that moral valence (obligations vs violations) matters for direction and magnitude of effects <cite id="1b59dcd9-0">A systematic review of 114 experiments finds that definitions of ‘moral,’ differences in frame valence (obligations vs violations), and diverse outcomes capturing cognitive, affective, and perceived polarization are critical; visual and multimodal manipulations and non-moral control groups also shape results</cite><cite id="1b59dcd9-2">Moral framing experiments often draw on moral foundations theory but face internal and external validity concerns; clarifying ‘moral’ and moral theories is needed to understand when, why, and which moral frames impact polarization</cite>. These patterns imply that framings which map cross-attitudinal moral obligations (e.g., unity, civic duty) are more likely to reduce polarization, whereas framings that accent cross-attitudinal violations (e.g., unfairness, betrayal of moral norms) are more likely to increase it, depending on how audiences map the cues onto their core moralized identities <cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Differences in moral valence and multimodal cues affect whether framing depolarizes or polarizes, with outcomes that capture affective and perceived polarization</cite><cite id="16e5448b-0">Rhetoric incongruent with prior attitudes evokes negative affect and predicts opinion change</cite>.

# Which Matters Most: Mechanisms and Comparative Strength

- Affective feelings (private and expressed) are foundational predictors because they shape how audiences interpret congruence and opposition, and they modulate persuasion via motivated reasoning and identity threat pathways. Physiological and experimental evidence shows that elicited negative affect reliably shifts evaluations and preferences, suggesting that elite cues which reliably trigger moral outrage or contempt will disproportionately drive mass affective polarization compared to neutral or issue-only cues <cite id="3478dea0-0">Identity performances and socially constructed judgments of alignment/antagonism underpin polarization, and surveys abstract from these communicative processes</cite><cite id="16e5448b-0">Negative affect from incongruent rhetoric predicts opinion change, independent of reported emotions</cite>. 

- Strategic framing that leverages moral schemas can outperform issue-only messaging in both reach and persistence because moral frames activate core affect and social identity appraisals. Where moral valence is violated (elite rhetoric portraying opponents as violating shared moral norms), polarization rises; where moral valence is affirmed (shared values, civic virtue), polarization falls. Thus, moral framing is often the most potent mechanism among elites’ tools, not because it is inherently partisan, but because it taps universalized identities and emotions that unify or cleave audiences depending on valence and congruence <cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Moral frame valence and multimodal cues determine direction of polarization effects; outcomes should distinguish affective and perceived polarization</cite><cite id="16e5448b-1">Emphasizing moral behaviors of out-party members reduces polarization by highlighting a joint value base</cite>.

- Public rhetoric’s effect sizes depend on tonal valence and audience trust. Respectful, congenial rhetoric from elites can measurably reduce negative emotions and social distance, offering a high-leverage depolarization tool that is robust to politician–audience partisan alignment and does not require high baseline trust, which makes it comparatively easy to deploy at scale relative to institutional reforms <cite id="3478dea0-1">Politicians’ congenial messages reduce negative emotions and social distance toward outpartisans without requiring alignment or high trust</cite>.

In short, private affect among elites is a necessary background condition: when out-party hate is high, mass affective polarization is structurally primed and more responsive to affective cues in public discourse. Public rhetoric and strategic framing act as catalysts: issue-only messaging can shift beliefs but often fails to change feelings and intergroup attitudes; moralized rhetoric can either amplify or attenuate polarization depending on whether it signals violations or shared obligations. Among mechanisms, moral framing and affective rhetoric typically matter most because they directly target core identity feelings and social-cognitive schemas, producing larger and more durable shifts in mass affective polarization than issue-technical frames, with tone and valence determining direction rather than mechanism per se <cite id="16e5448b-0">Affective responses to rhetoric predict change and are amplified by incongruence and arousal</cite><cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Moral framing experiments highlight valence and multimodal features as determinants of polarization outcomes</cite><cite id="3478dea0-1">Congenial elite rhetoric reduces negative emotions and social distance</cite><cite id="3478dea0-2">Affective polarization globally skews toward out-party hate, indicating a receptive backdrop for affective cues</cite>.

# Boundaries, Trade-offs, and Open Questions

- Elite rhetoric can depolarize quickly but may also be co-opted or drowned out by partisan feedback loops; globally, a persistent imbalance toward out-party hate implies that polarizing affective cues will have outsized influence unless counter-framing and congenial moral appeals are scaled systematically <cite id="3478dea0-2">Out-party hate has grown relative to in-party love across Western democracies</cite>.

- Moral framing’s potency depends on audience mapping of violations vs obligations. Reviews caution that many experiments conflate frames or undertheorize “moral,” leading to inconsistent sign predictions; clarifying moral definitions and valence is essential to reliably predict when moral frames will depolarize vs polarize <cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Calls for clearer definitions of ‘moral,’ attention to valence, and broader outcome measures to capture cognitive, affective, and perceived polarization</cite><cite id="1b59dcd9-2">Moral foundations theory faces validity concerns; expanding moral theories can improve precision</cite>.

- Private feelings measures are predictive but incomplete: surveys capture levels and changes over time yet omit identity performances and interactional cues through which elites shape mass affect. Triangulating survey-based affect with experimental manipulations of elite rhetoric and framing, and with content analyses of legislative discourse, offers the strongest forecasts of mass polarization trajectories <cite id="3478dea0-0">Survey measures abstract from identity performances and framing effects, with responses sensitive to question framing</cite>.

Practical implication: To differentially predict and reduce mass polarization, elites should prioritize congenial, identity-bridging moral frames that affirm shared obligations and model prosocial behavior, while minimizing rhetoric that reliably elicits moral outrage or contempt across divides. Where institutional polarization is high (as reflected in private affect and elite antagonism), moral framing and respectful rhetoric offer comparatively high-leverage levers to shift the affective baseline, whereas issue-only messaging alone will be insufficient to change feelings and intergroup attitudes <cite id="3478dea0-1">Congenial elite rhetoric reduces negative emotions and social distance toward outpartisans</cite><cite id="16e5448b-1">Moral behaviors of out-party members reduce affective polarization</cite><cite id="3478dea0-2">Out-party hate’s dominance underscores the need for elite signals that rebalance affect</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Yes—different operationalizations of elite affective polarization differentially predict mass polarization. Private feelings set the baseline; public rhetoric and strategic framing shift it by activating moral schemas and intergroup emotions. <cite id="3478dea0-0">Survey-based private affect measures capture core feelings but omit communicative performances that shape polarization</cite><cite id="16e5448b-0">Rhetoric that incongruent with prior attitudes elicits negative affect and drives change</cite>.

- Among mechanisms, moral framing and affect-laden rhetoric matter most because they directly target identity and moral emotions, producing larger, more durable shifts; congenial moral signals from elites can depolarize, while moral-violation cues polarize. <cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Moral valence and multimodal cues determine whether framing depolarizes or polarizes</cite><cite id="3478dea0-1">Respectful elite rhetoric reduces negative emotions and social distance</cite><cite id="16e5448b-1">Moral behaviors of out-partisans reduce polarization</cite>.

- Measurement and scope: Use private-affect surveys to track baselines, content analyses of elite rhetoric to quantify moral/affective valence, and randomized experiments to estimate causal effects on mass affect and social distance—then triangulate which elite cues move the needle most in each context <cite id="3478dea0-0">Survey measures must be interpreted alongside identity performances and framing effects</cite><cite id="1b59dcd9-0">Experiments should better theorize ‘moral’ and report affective and perceived polarization outcomes</cite>. </answer>

Title: How language divides: Asymmetries in the differentiating power of opinion discourse
Snippet: Despite its diversity, research on polarization in social psychology shares a common methodological feature: heavy reliance on survey responses. Affective polarization (Iyengar et al., 2012) is typically measured using instruments such as the "feeling thermometer" (Gidron et al., 2022), while political and opinion polarization are assessed through rating scales capturing attitudes toward social groups or policy positions. Although polarization is "most properly understood as a description of the distribution of a population" (Bakker & Lelkes, 2024, p. 419), it is frequently operationalized as an individual-difference variable. Participants are asked to rate how warm or cold they feel toward ingroups and outgroups, and the difference between these ratings is treated as a proxy for polarization (e.g., Kingzette et al., 2021;Wakefield & Wakefield, 2023). These scores are then used as predictors or outcomes in linear models, abstracting polarization from its social and communicative context. 

This approach allows researchers to observe patterns of attitudinal congruence and divergence, but it overlooks how people judge group affiliation and opinion similarity in everyday settings (cf. Durrheim, 2022;Durrheim et al., 2016). By eliciting privately expressed attitudes, surveys estimate mental states within a broader distribution, yet they do not examine the identity performances (Klein et al., 2007) through which individuals publicly signal their views and interpret those of others. Such judgments are foundational: they enable actors to perceive alignment and opposition and thereby construct the shared opinion structures that make polarization possible. 

A deeper problem concerns measurement validity. Research shows that responses to rating scales often fail to map straightforwardly onto real-world expression (Potter, 1998). Survey answers vary with framing and question order (Rockwood et al., 1997), and it is often unclear which targets or dimensions respondents invoke when answering measures of affective polarization (Druckman & Levendusky, 2019). What is measured depends heavily on how categories are constructed and interpreted-processes that remain opaque within the instrument itself. In everyday interaction, individuals contradict themselves, articulate nuanced positions, and adjust their views across contexts.

Title: Congenial messages from politicians reduce affective polarization among citizens
Snippet: Affective polarization among citizens is often attributed to the harsh rhetoric and personal attacks that politicians direct at one another. However, the influence of elite rhetoric on affective polarization may work in both directions. We theorize that politicians can reduce affective polarization by making positive or respectful statements about their political opponents. A preregistered survey experiment with 2,000 citizens provides strong support for this expectation. Politicians’ congenial messages about their opponents significantly reduce affective polarization on two distinct measures. Specifically, the experimental treatments reduce citizens’ negative emotions toward outpartisans, as well as their desire to socially distance themselves from such outpartisans. The depolarizing effect of such messages does not depend on the political alignment of either the politician or the citizen, nor does it necessarily require high levels of political trust.

Title: In-Party Love, Out-Party Hate, and Affective Polarization in Twelve Established Democracies
Snippet: Abstract Recent research has mapped levels of affective polarization worldwide. However, our current knowledge of the longitudinal patterns of in- and out-party affect, the two constitutive terms of affective polarization, remains limited. This manuscript expands the comparative and longitudinal scope of existing studies using national election study data from 143 elections across 12 Western democracies collected since the 1960s. The analysis expands previous descriptive accounts of levels of in- and out-party affect, reports levels of in-party love and out-party hate, and inspects longitudinal changes in the polarity of affect with a composite measure tapping the relative weight of in- and out-party feelings. The findings show a generalized decline of out-party evaluations and a growing prevalence of out-party hate versus in-party love over time. While citizens may not be more polarized than before in most Western democracies, contemporary affective polarization is more heavily characterized by a disproportionate weight of out-group dislike.

Title: Learning to Like the Enemy: Moral Learning Reduces Affective Polarization
Snippet: As affective polarization, an identity-defining attitude (Dias & Lelkes, 2022), has increased, treatments mitigating the disapproval of political opponents are sorely needed. Our results across three experiments showed that exposure to moral behaviors of out-party members effectively reduces polarization. These findings are important for policymakers and civil society interested in fighting affective polarization. Highlighting the moral behavior of out-party members and thereby emphasizing the joint value base of all citizens could be effectively implemented in future campaigns or educational programs aiming to fight affective polarization. For example, social media clips can present real-life examples of people who put themselves in danger to help others while noting their political affiliation. Finally, the moral learning treatment can be applied to other conflict areas, such as post-war reconciliation or the reduction of prejudice.

However, the influence of elite rhetoric on affective polarization may work in both directions. We theorize that politicians can reduce affective polarization by making positive or respectful statements about their political opponents. A preregistered survey experiment with 2,000 citizens provides strong support for this expectation. Politicians’ congenial messages about their opponents significantly reduce affective polarization on two distinct measures. Specifically, the experimental treatments reduce citizens’ negative emotions toward outpartisans, as well as their desire to socially distance themselves from such outpartisans. The depolarizing effect of such messages does not depend on the political alignment of either the politician or the citizen, nor does it necessarily require high levels of political trust.

Title: How the effects of emphasizing ethics are examined: a systematic review of moral framing experiments
Snippet: ABSTRACT Whether and when moral frames (de)polarize society is a matter of scholarly debate. To identify key research priorities for advancing our understanding of moral framing effects, a systematic review of 114 experiments was conducted. The study explored the use of important theoretical and methodological approaches and compared them between studies belonging to the most salient communication fields in experimental moral framing research. Based on the results, this paper advocates for more attention in moral framing experiments to (a) definitions of the term ‘moral’, (b) differences in frame valence (i.e. moral obligations vs. violations), (c) diverse outcomes that capture distinct types of polarization (i.e. cognitive, affective, perceived), (d) visual and multimodal manipulations, and (e) the choice of non-moral control group(s).

Title: Virtue or passion? How moral frames in climate change appeals elicit emotions and change opinions
Snippet: Respondents exposed to a PRR moral climate appeal are more likely to agree with the PRR climate diagnosis and solutions compared to respondents to a non-moral climate appeal. 

Our following set of hypotheses argues that the framing effect only takes place when individuals are emotionally aroused by the moral climate appeal-that is, it is passion that drives the effect. If moral climate frames are processed emotionally, we would expect that exposure to such a frame does not immediately lead to agreement with diagnosis and solutions, but that an emotional response is necessary. This perspective aligns with moral psychological research arguing that the impact of information on a moral transgression on our evaluation of that transgression is expected to be processed affectively (Greene et al., 2001). Research shows that moral appeals in political elite rhetoric facilitate emotional processing, in such a way that these appeals elicit emotions (Ciuk & Rottman, 2020;Clifford, 2019;Jung, 2020;Lipsitz, 2018). In line with these findings, we first of all assume that climate viewpoints appealing to morality will elicit emotions among respondents, compared to a viewpoint that is not explicitly moral. We thus propose the following hypothesis: 

H2. Exposure to a moral climate appeal, regardless of its nature, triggers stronger emotions than exposure to non-moral climate appeal. 

In a next step, we investigate whether specific moral climate appeals will elicit the dominant emotions that are discursively embedded in them, as laid out in Table 1: H3.1. Exposure to a mainstream climate appeal elicits more fear than exposure to a non-moral climate appeal.

Title: How the effects of emphasizing ethics are examined: a systematic review of moral framing experiments
Snippet: This systematic review first of all reveals a need for stronger theoretical foundations of experiments on moral framing effects. In the case of over half of the included studies, no reference was made to any moral theory in the theory sections of the corresponding publications, which indicated insufficient scholarly attention to the complexities of defining morality sufficiently clearly and precisely. It should be noted that many of the experiments included did not exclusively test moral framing effects. They often focused on testing the effects of multiple types of frames at the same time (e.g. Rees et al., 2022, compared the effects of a moral frame to those of a business frame). This may explain the lack of theoretical accounts of morality. Nonetheless, to move experimental moral framing research forward, it is important to dedicate more effort to conceptualizing the term 'moral'. By reducing ambiguity and enhancing uniformity in what we consider to be instances of moral framing, researchers will better comprehend when, why, and which moral frames impact polarization dynamics. 

Most experiments that were embedded in moral theory used moral foundations theory (Graham et al., 2009). These studies have gained valuable insights into how different moral foundations could serve as framing devices. However, concerns have been raised regarding both the internal validity (e.g. the liberal-conservative dichotomy, Janoff-Bulman & Carnes, 2013) and external validity (e.g. the generalizability to different groups of people, Davis et al., 2016) of moral foundations theory. It would therefore be highly beneficial for experimental framing research to extend its scope and focus more on other moral theories and models as well. 4 This would allow framing researchers to explore the complexities and nuances of moral reasoning and decision-making beyond the specific foundations emphasized in moral foundations theory. 

These recommendations apply not only to experimental moral-framing research in general but also hold particular relevance for studies on corporate communication. When compared to political and environmental communication, experiments on moral framing and corporate communication seemed to be lagging behind in sufficiently substantiating hypotheses based on theory that is specifically aimed at explaining and predicting moral emotions, cognitions, and behaviors. Conducting more moral theory-driven experiments presents a promising opportunity for this body of research.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer attempts to distinguish the three operationalizations but fails to meet the criterion's requirements. While it discusses 'private feelings,' 'public rhetoric,' and 'strategic framing' as separate concepts, it does not provide evidence that the cited studies measure them as distinct independent variables. The answer conflates these dimensions throughout—for example, treating 'moral framing' as a type of strategic framing while also discussing it as a feature of public rhetoric, and treating private affect as both a 'background condition' and something that operates through public discourse. Critically, the answer does not provide (a) specific comparative evidence with effect sizes or experimental contrasts showing one operationalization predicts mass polarization more strongly than others while holding other factors constant, nor does it (b) explicitly state that existing research conflates these operationalizations and lacks the needed controlled comparisons. Instead, it asserts that 'moral framing and affect-laden rhetoric matter most' without evidence that any study actually varied these operationalizations independently. The studies cited measure outcomes of different elite communication strategies (congenial messages [4], moral behaviors [5], moral frames [6][7]) but do not isolate whether effects stem from private elite feelings, public rhetoric tone, or strategic framing logic as distinct causal mechanisms.
other_issues: Structural confusion: The answer treats the three operationalizations as overlapping rather than as distinct, measurable constructs. For example, 'moral framing' is discussed as both strategic framing and as a feature of public rhetoric, making it impossible to determine which operationalization is being tested.

Lack of measurement differentiation: The answer does not explain how any study measures 'private feelings' of elites (as opposed to mass publics), making claims about elite private feelings as predictors unsupported.

Missing comparative evidence: No study cited actually compares the relative predictive power of the three operationalizations. Study [4] tests congenial vs. non-congenial rhetoric, [5] tests moral behavior exposure, [6] is a review, [7] tests moral vs. non-moral frames—but none isolate whether effects are due to elite private feelings, rhetorical tone, or strategic frame choice as independent variables.
Assertion without evidence: The conclusion that 'moral framing and affective rhetoric matter most' is not supported by any study that holds other factors constant while varying operationalization.

Misuse of citations: Reference [1] discusses measurement of mass affective polarization via surveys, not how to measure elite affective polarization's different operationalizations. Reference [2] measures mass-level in-party/out-party affect longitudinally, not elite-level private feelings.

Conceptual slippage: The answer shifts between discussing elite affect as a cause and mass affect as an outcome without clearly delineating the causal chain or providing evidence that studies measure elite-level operationalizations distinctly.
judgment.summary: The answer attempts to address the question but fundamentally fails the verification criterion. It does not demonstrate that studies measure the three operationalizations (private feelings, public rhetoric, strategic framing) as distinct, comparable constructs, nor does it provide controlled comparative evidence of differential predictive power. Instead, it treats these as overlapping features of elite communication and makes unsupported assertions about which 'matters most.' The answer would need either (a) evidence from studies that experimentally vary operationalization while holding content constant, or (b) an explicit acknowledgment that existing research conflates these dimensions and cannot answer the question.
